description: How to break a screen into components and decide where state lives.

screens.body:
Before writing anything, sketch the screen and draw boxes around the pieces: the header, the search bar, the list, each card. Those boxes become your components.

Naming the pieces first keeps you from building one giant tangled component and splitting it later in a panic.

options: Sketch the UI and box up the pieces
check.question: What's the first step of thinking in React?

screens.heading: Start from the UI, not the code
screens.keyPoint: Boxes on the mock → components in the code.

screens.body:
A component should do one thing well: a Button renders a button, a SearchBar handles searching. When a component starts doing three jobs, split it.

Small components are easier to test, easier to reuse, and much easier to read at 2 AM.

options: When it's doing more than one job
check.question: When should you split a component?

screens.heading: One job per component

screens.body:
Props flow one way: from parent to child. A child can read what the parent passes, but it can't reach up and change the parent's data.

This one-way flow is what makes React apps predictable — you can always trace where data came from by walking up the tree.

options: Down: parent to child via props
check.question: Which way does data flow in React?

screens.heading: Data flows down

screens.body:
Children can't change parent data directly — but the parent can hand down a callback prop like onSave. The child calls it, the parent does the updating.

So: data flows down as props, changes flow up as callbacks. Two directions, two different mechanisms.

options: By calling a callback prop the parent passed down
By editing the parent's state directly
check.question: How does a child tell its parent something happened?

screens.heading: Events flow up

screens.body:
When two sibling components need the same data — a search box and its results list — neither should own it. Move the state to their shared parent and pass it down to both.

This is called lifting state up, and it's the most common React refactor you'll ever do.

options: Lift the state to their shared parent
check.question: Two siblings need the same data. What do you do?

screens.heading: Lift state up
screens.keyPoint: Shared data lives in the closest shared parent.

screens.body:
Rendering the same markup twice? That's a component waiting to be born. Pull it out, give it props for the parts that vary, and render it in a loop.

Lists especially: map over your data and render one <Card /> per item instead of copy-pasting markup.

options: Make a Card component and render it per item
Put it all in one giant div
check.question: You render the same card markup three times. Best move?

screens.heading: Repetition becomes a component

screens.body:
For every piece of data, ask who owns it. If only one component uses it, keep the state there. If several need it, lift it up. If it's passed in and never changed locally, it's a prop.

State = owned and changeable. Props = borrowed and read-only. That one question settles most design debates.

check.question: Data used by one component only should be…

screens.heading: Ask: who owns this data?
screens.keyPoint: 'Who owns this?' settles state vs props.
